groups.text: Here is a settlement job, written the usual way.
One loop reads the clock, loads payments, skips refunds, holds recent ones, sums per merchant, computes fees, calls the payout A P I, and saves the ledger.
It works. But to test one fee rule, you need a fixed clock, a fake store, a fake payout A P I, and checks on what the fakes recorded.
Look at the colours.
The teal lines only decide.
The gold lines touch the world.
Pull them apart: the decisions go into a core, and the I O wraps around it.
The core is a pure function.
It takes plain values, today's date included, and returns a plan: a value that says what should happen.
This shape is called a functional core and an imperative shell.
Here is the smallest one, from the lesson.
Card authorizations older than seven days get voided.
The shell reads the clock, and loads two: aone, eight days old, and atwo, thirty hours old.
It hands them to the core as values.
The core returns two decisions: void aone, and keep atwo, with one hundred thirty-eight hours left.
It called nothing, and read no clock.
Then the shell carries out the plan: one call to the gateway.
A test needs none of the shell.
Call the core with a list and a date, one day later, and compare the result.
atwo is still kept, now with one hundred fourteen hours left.
All of this needs inputs that hold still.
A read-only List does not promise that.
Build a batch from the caller's list, and both point at the same list.
The caller adds ptwo.
The batch shows pone and ptwo: it changed under your feet.
Copy at the boundary.
With toList in Kotlin, or List.copyOf in Java, the batch keeps its own snapshot.
In code, the shell is three steps: read, decide, act.
The same in Kotlin and in Java.
So: the core decides from plain values, and the shell does the I O around it.
A quick check.
A teammate reads the clock inside the core.
Is it still pure?
No. The clock is a hidden input, so the same arguments can give a different plan.
Read it in the shell, and pass today in.
